title: A clock request through the secure world

steps.title: Enabling one clock takes a trip into the secure world
steps.body:
Six lanes, left to right, are the actors: three Linux layers at EL1, then BL31 (the EL3 monitor), the OP-TEE core (SCMI server at S-EL1) and the clock hardware. Time runs downward; teal arrows are the normal world, rose arrows the secure world, dashed arrows the return.

The example: the SD card driver wants its clock on. SCMI is Arm's System Control and Management Interface, a message protocol; here it is carried by `smc`, the instruction that crosses into the secure world.

steps.title: 1. The SD card driver asks for its kernel clock
steps.body:
During `mmci_probe()` the driver calls `clk_prepare_enable(ck_ker_sdmmc1)`. The call lands in `clk-stm32mp25`, Linux's RCC (Reset and Clock Control) driver.

Without this clock the SD controller cannot work, and the root filesystem is on that card.

steps.title: 2-3. The parent clock is an SCMI clock, so Linux asks for it first
steps.body:
The gate `ck_ker_sdmmc1` has parent `flexgen_51`, which is an SCMI clock. The framework enables the parent first with `clk_enable(parent)`, which reaches `scmi_clk_enable()` in `clk-scmi`.

Linux can only manage gates and dividers below clocks the secure world owns.

steps.title: 4. The request becomes an SCMI message
steps.body:
`clk-scmi` and `arm_scmi` build a message for clock protocol `0x14` using `CLOCK_CONFIG_SET` (`0x7`) with the enable setting.

The message names a protocol, a message id and parameters, and the reply carries a status.

steps.title: 5. The message crosses to the secure world as an smc
steps.body:
The transport is an `smc` with `OPTEE_SMC_CALL_WITH_ARG`, which carries a call to the PTA-SCMI pseudo trusted application, command 1, `PROCESS_SMT_CHANNEL`. A pseudo trusted application is a service built into OP-TEE itself.

The `smc` instruction traps to EL3, so BL31 receives it first.

steps.title: 6-7. BL31 enters S-EL1 and the SCMI server decodes the message
steps.body:
BL31's `opteed_smc_handler` saves the normal-world context and does an ERET (exception return) into S-EL1, where OP-TEE runs. In OP-TEE, `pta/scmi.c` passes the message to `scmi_server`, and `scmi_clock` maps it to `optee_clock`.

BL31 only forwards; it does not understand the clock message.

steps.title: 8. OP-TEE enables the generator in the clock hardware
steps.body:
OP-TEE uses its own secure-world access to the RCC to enable the flexgen output.

Normal-world code cannot do this itself, which is the point: the root and bus clocks are owned by the secure side.

steps.title: The status travels back the same way
steps.body:
OP-TEE puts the status in the shared buffer and returns from the `smc`. BL31 returns to NS-EL1 (non-secure EL1), `clk-scmi` returns 0, and the RCC driver finally sets its own gate bit.

Only then does the probe go on.

steps.title: The device tree wires Linux to OP-TEE
steps.body:
The `optee` node uses `method = "smc"`. The `scmi` node with `compatible = "linaro,scmi-optee"` offers protocols `0x14` (clocks), `0x16` (resets) and `0x17` (voltage domains).

Without the `scmi` node Linux would have no clock provider for these roots.

steps.anchor: Why does a clock need a round trip?
steps.title: Takeaway: the secure world owns the roots of the clock tree
steps.body:
HSE, HSI, the ICN bus clocks and the FLEXGEN outputs are owned by OP-TEE. The `rcc` node lists them as inputs from `scmi_clk`, and Linux manages only the gates and dividers below them.

The same ideas are drawn for the i.MX 8M Plus in the diagrams **What happens on an smc** (`smc-flow`) and **How TrustZone is enforced** (`trustzone`).
